cls: Antipsychotic (substituted benzamide; selective D2/D3 dopamine antagonist)
pharm: Selective dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist with regional selectivity for limbic areas; used for agitation, alcohol withdrawal, and movement disorders
quick: Agitation/aggression: 200-300 mg/day in divided doses; alcohol withdrawal: 300-1200 mg/day; movement disorders: 300-800 mg/day
May be taken with or without food
Not recommended unless clearly necessary; monitor neonate for extrapyramidal/withdrawal signs
Excretion in human milk not established; avoid unless essential
Avoid alcohol-containing preparations; additive CNS effects
ECG/QT, electrolytes, prolactin, EPS, blood counts
summary: Tiapride is a substituted benzamide that selectively antagonises dopamine D2 and D3 receptors, with relatively high regional selectivity for limbic areas. It is used to manage agitation and aggression (particularly in the elderly and in chronic alcoholism), alcohol withdrawal syndrome, and hyperkinetic movement disorders such as chorea, tardive dyskinesia, and tics. It is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys, so the dose must be reduced according to creatinine clearance. Key risks include extrapyramidal symptoms, dose-dependent QT prolongation, hyperprolactinaemia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
indications: Agitation and aggressive behaviour, particularly in elderly patients and in chronic alcoholism
Movement disorders including chorea (e.g., Huntington's disease), tardive dyskinesia, and tics

dosage.d: 200-300 mg/day in divided doses, up to 400 mg/day; typically for 1-2 months
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration; reassess regularly

dosage.d: Start 50 mg twice daily; increase by 50-100 mg every 2-3 days to a maximum of about 300 mg/day
dosage.n: Elderly are more susceptible to sedation, EPS, and hypotension

dosage.d: 300-400 mg/day for acute withdrawal; higher ranges of 400-1200 mg/day (up to 1800 mg/day if necessary) are described
dosage.n: Titrate to symptom severity and taper as the patient stabilises

dosage.d: Reduce daily dose by creatinine clearance: 75% of normal at CrCl 50-80 mL/min, 50% at 10-50 mL/min, 25% at below 10 mL/min
dosage.n: Tiapride is excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys

admin: Give in divided doses through the day; titrate gradually, especially in the elderly
Obtain a baseline ECG and electrolytes before treatment in patients with cardiac risk factors
Reduce the dose according to creatinine clearance in renal impairment
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration and review need regularly
Avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use, particularly in chorea (risk of withdrawal worsening)
moa: Tiapride is a substituted benzamide that selectively blocks dopamine D2 and D3 receptors. It shows relatively high regional selectivity for limbic over striatal areas, which is thought to underlie its useful effect on agitation and hyperkinetic movement disorders with a comparatively lower liability for some extrapyramidal effects at therapeutic doses. Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade raises prolactin.

absolute: Concomitant levodopa or other dopaminergic agents
relative: Cardiovascular disease, bradycardia, congenital or acquired QT prolongation, electrolyte disturbance
Elderly with dementia (increased mortality with antipsychotics)
Risk factors for stroke or venous thromboembolism
monitor: Full blood count for signs of dyscrasia

preg: There are no adequate data on the use of tiapride in pregnant women, and animal studies have shown reproductive toxicity. Neonates exposed during the third trimester may experience extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms. Tiapride should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary, with neonatal monitoring.
lact: It is not known whether tiapride is excreted in human breast milk. Because of insufficient safety data, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment unless considered essential.
renal: Tiapride is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys (approximately 70% excreted unchanged in urine). The daily dose should be reduced according to creatinine clearance: about 75% of the normal dose at CrCl 50-80 mL/min, 50% at CrCl 10-50 mL/min, and 25% at CrCl below 10 mL/min.
hepatic: Tiapride undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, so no specific dose adjustment is generally required in hepatic impairment. Use clinical judgement and the lowest effective dose.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs such as class IA/III antiarrhythmics, methadone, certain antipsychotics and antimicrobials (additive torsades risk)
Drugs causing bradycardia or hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia (increase torsades de pointes risk)
moderate: CNS depressants, opioids, benzodiazepines, antihistamines, anaesthetics (additive sedation)
Other dopamine antagonists (additive EPS and prolactin elevation)
minor: Antacids and sucralfate may reduce absorption if taken together (separate dosing)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol and alcohol-containing preparations; additive central nervous system depression
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum prolactin and may interfere with prolactin-related investigations

serious: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
rare: Hyponatraemia / syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness, raised creatine kinase) - discontinue immediately and provide emergency supportive care
Syncope, palpitations, or arrhythmia suggesting torsades de pointes - urgent ECG and correction of electrolytes

monitoring: ECG / QT interval at baseline and with dose changes in at-risk patients
Serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), correcting deficits before/during therapy
Serum prolactin, especially with symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia
Extrapyramidal symptoms and signs of tardive dyskinesia
Renal function (creatinine clearance) to guide dosing
Full blood count if signs of infection or unexplained fever
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed in divided doses; do not stop suddenly without medical advice
Report fever with muscle stiffness, palpitations, fainting, or unusual movements promptly
Avoid alcohol because it increases drowsiness
Be aware of possible breast changes, milk production, or menstrual/sexual changes from raised prolactin
Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how the drug affects you
Tell your doctor about kidney problems and any heart-rhythm conditions
pk: Calming effect generally within hours of oral dosing
Peak plasma concentration about 0.4 to 1.5 hours after an oral dose
Short; usually requires divided daily dosing to maintain effect
Store below 25 C in original packaging; protect from moisture (follow product label)
pearls: Not FDA-approved; this information is derived from EMA/SmPC (e.g., French/EU labelling) and BNF/manufacturer prescribing sources
Useful for agitation/aggression in the elderly and in chronic alcoholism, alcohol withdrawal, and hyperkinetic movement disorders
Largely renally cleared - reduce dose by creatinine clearance (75%/50%/25% bands)
Short half-life (about 3 hours) and oral bioavailability around 75%; negligible plasma protein binding
Carries QT-prolongation, EPS, hyperprolactinaemia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk like other benzamides
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Experience is limited and there is no specific antidote. Features may include drowsiness, sedation, extrapyramidal reactions, hypotension, and dose-dependent QT prolongation with risk of arrhythmia. Management is supportive with cardiac/ECG monitoring, correction of electrolytes, and anticholinergic agents for severe dystonic reactions. Tiapride is only poorly removed by dialysis. Contact a poison control centre.
